subject: ENG
label: Grade 08
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 08 English, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 7 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Prose and drama
modules.outcome: compare how two writers show the same theme
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Prose and drama', taught in a way that is with notes, a worked line and a self-mark. The target is clear: compare how two writers show the same theme. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Prose and drama' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: compare how two writers show the same theme, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Main idea in one sentence. Character: what they say and do shows what they are like (she gave away her lunch: generous). Drama: names on the left, stage directions in brackets. Method: Model run for 'Prose and drama'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Compare how two writers show the same theme: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Read Extract A. 'My knees shook on the diving board. Below, the water was a blue blade. I counted: three, two, one. I jumped.' It is told by the narrator, 'I', in short sentences. The action happens quickly and the reader feels the speed.

Step 2, Read Extract B. 'Mira stood at the edge of the stage like a small lighthouse in a storm of faces. Her voice, when it came, was thin as thread, but it did not break.' This is third person, with a long sentence and a simile. The reader watches from outside.

Step 3, Identify the shared theme. Both extracts show courage in facing fear: the diver's fear of heights and Mira's fear of an audience. State it as a sentence: 'Courage means acting while still afraid.' Evidence: 'knees shook... I jumped' and 'thin as thread, but it did not break'.

Step 4, Compare the techniques. A uses first person and short, quick sentences to build tension, plus the metaphor 'a blue blade'. B uses third person and a simile, 'like a small lighthouse', to make Mira look small but steady. A feels immediate, whereas B feels reflective.

Step 5, Write a comparative paragraph. 'Both writers show courage in facing fear. In A, the countdown and short sentences create suspense, whereas in B the simile of a lighthouse makes Mira seem small yet strong. Therefore A presents courage as a quick leap and B as steady endurance.'

Step 6, Your turn: compare two lines on loneliness: A 'The house was quiet. I talked to the clock.' B 'Kai sat on the bench like a stone, while the crowd flowed around him.' Model answer: Both show loneliness; A uses first person and a short, plain voice, whereas B uses a simile and an outside view to show isolation.

modules.title: Tenses, voice and modals
modules.outcome: use tenses, voice and modals precisely
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Tenses, voice and modals', taught in a way that is with notes, a worked line and a self-mark. The target is clear: use tenses, voice and modals precisely. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Tenses, voice and modals' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: use tenses, voice and modals precisely, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Passive: 'The cat chased the mouse' becomes 'The mouse was chased by the cat.' Reported: 'I will come,' she said becomes She said that she would come. Modals: 'should' for advice, 'must' for rules. Agreement: 'The list of items is long.' Edit: 'He go to school' becomes 'He goes to school.' Method: Model run for 'Tenses, voice and modals'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Use tenses, voice and modals precisely: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Review the tenses with a timeline. Past perfect: 'She had left before I arrived.' Present perfect continuous: 'I have been studying for two hours.' Future perfect: 'By June, we will have finished.' Say which action came first and which came second.

Step 2, Use modals for ability, advice and obligation. 'You must wear a helmet' (obligation). 'You should sleep early' (advice). 'She can swim' (ability). 'He may arrive late' (possibility). The verb after a modal is always the base form: 'must wear', not 'must wears'.

Step 3, Use modals about the past. 'He might have missed the bus' (possibility). 'You should have called' (regret or advice). 'They could have won' (it was possible, but did not happen). Form: modal plus have plus the past participle.

Step 4, Use modals in the passive. Active: 'You must finish the work.' Passive: 'The work must be finished.' Active: 'They should have repaired it.' Passive: 'It should have been repaired.' Pattern: modal plus be plus past participle, or have been plus past participle.

Step 5, Check precision. 'You must park here' is a rule, 'you should park here' is advice and 'you may park here' is permission. A different modal changes the meaning. Read each sentence aloud and ask what the speaker means.

Step 6, Your turn: (a) rewrite in the passive: 'We must clean the lab.' (b) fill in: 'I am not certain, but he (might/must) have forgotten.' Answer: (a) The lab must be cleaned. (b) might have forgotten, because 'might' shows possibility, while 'must' would show certainty.

modules.title: Descriptive and narrative writing
modules.outcome: write with detail and varied sentence openings
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Descriptive and narrative writing', taught in a way that is with notes, a worked line and a self-mark. The target is clear: write with detail and varied sentence openings. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Descriptive and narrative writing' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: write with detail and varied sentence openings, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Topic sentence: 'My school library is my favourite place.' Details: quiet, shelves of picture books, a reading corner. Closing: 'I visit it every Friday.' For narrative use first, then, suddenly, finally. Method: Model run for 'Descriptive and narrative writing'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Write with detail and varied sentence openings: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Begin with a plain sentence and improve it. 'The boy walked into the market. It was crowded.' It is correct but flat. Detail means adding sights, sounds, smells and exact verbs, and varied openings stop every sentence from starting with 'The'.

Step 2, Add detail with exact words. 'The boy edged into the market, where fruit sellers called out prices and the smell of ripe mangoes hung in the heat.' 'Edged' is more exact than 'walked', and the extra clause adds sound and smell.

Step 3, Vary the sentence openings. Start with an adverb: 'Slowly, he pushed through the crowd.' An -ing word: 'Clutching his coins, he searched for the bakery.' A prepositional phrase: 'Between the stalls, a thin cat darted.' A clause: 'Although he was hungry, he did not hurry.'

Step 4, Put it together as a short narrative. 'Slowly, he pushed through the crowd. Clutching his coins, he searched for the bakery. Between the stalls, a thin cat darted past, and the smell of fresh bread led him on.' Each sentence opens differently, yet the scene stays connected.

Step 5, Edit. Read the passage and check that no two sentences in a row start with the same word. Replace vague words (nice, big, said). Keep the past tense. Cut any detail that does not add to the picture, because more detail is not always better.

Step 6, Your turn: improve 'The girl ran to the bus. She was late.' using two different openings. Model answer: 'Panting, the girl sprinted towards the bus. Although she was late, she did not give up, and the doors slid shut just as her hand touched the rail.'

modules.title: Poetry
modules.outcome: read a poem closely and write a short critical response
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Poetry', taught in a way that is with notes, a worked line and a self-mark. The target is clear: read a poem closely and write a short critical response. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Poetry' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: read a poem closely and write a short critical response, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Simile: 'The moon is like a silver coin.' Metaphor: 'The classroom was a zoo.' Imagery: 'the dew-wet grass' appeals to sight and touch. Say what feeling each creates. Method: Model run for 'Poetry'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Read a poem closely and write a short critical response: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Read the poem once for the sense. Poem: 'The old clock in the hall / counts hours no one wants. / Tick, it says, and tick again, / while dust sits in the sun.' Ask: who speaks, what is happening, how does it feel? Answer in one line: a clock keeps counting in an empty, quiet house.

Step 2, Read again and mark the language. 'Counts hours no one wants' gives the clock a human action, which is personification. 'Tick' repeated twice copies the sound, so the poem feels slow. 'Dust sits in the sun' is a quiet visual image. Underline each and write a label in the margin.

Step 3, Ask what each choice does. The repeated 'tick' makes time feel endless and a little lonely. 'No one wants' tells us the hours are unwelcome, so the house is probably empty or sad. Soft sounds in 'sits in the sun' slow the last line, like the end of a day.

Step 4, Plan a response with Point, Evidence, Explain. Point: the poet builds a lonely mood. Evidence: 'counts hours no one wants'. Explain: giving the clock a job nobody values suggests time passing without company. Add a second paragraph on the repeated 'tick'.

Step 5, Write it. 'The poet creates a lonely mood by personifying the clock, which "counts hours no one wants". This suggests that time continues in an empty house, and the word "wants" hints at sadness. The repeated "tick" strengthens this by making the silence feel endless.' Check you quoted exactly.

Step 6, Your turn: write three sentences on the line 'dust sits in the sun'. Model answer: The image shows stillness, because dust usually drifts but here it 'sits'. The warm sun contrasts with the sad mood, suggesting beauty nobody notices. This supports the poem's idea of an empty, forgotten house.

modules.example: Solved: Formal letter: 12 November 2026; The Principal; Subject: request for a library card; 'Respected Sir, I am a student of Class 8...'; Yours faithfully, Aman. Informal: Dear Ria, ... Your friend, Aman. Report: title, date, place, what happened, result, writer's name. Method: Model run for 'Formal letters, reports and speeches'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Write a report and a short speech with purpose: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Plan a report on water use at school. A report states facts in a set order: title, introduction, findings, conclusion, recommendation. It is written in the third person, in plain formal English. Title: Report on Water Wastage in the School Washrooms. Name the date, the writer and the reader (the principal).

Step 2, Collect numbers. A survey of 120 students found that 78 had seen a tap left running, 30 had not, and 12 were unsure. Calculate: 78 out of 120 is 65 percent, 30 is 25 percent, 12 is 10 percent. Together they make 100 percent, so the data is consistent.

Step 3, Write the findings. 'The survey of 120 students showed that 65 percent had seen a tap left running.' Use short paragraphs and one fact per sentence. The conclusion states what the facts mean: wastage is common. The recommendation says what to do, such as fitting push-taps and putting up reminder posters.

Step 4, Switch to a speech, which is written to be heard. Purpose: persuade classmates to save water. Open with a hook: 'Every minute a tap runs, we can lose many litres of water.' Greet the audience properly, for example 'Respected principal, teachers and friends'. Keep sentences short so they are easy to follow.

Step 5, Build three points with the rule of three: first, wastage is common (65 percent saw it); second, it costs the school money; third, small habits fix it. Close with a call to action: 'Next time you see a running tap, turn it off. Thank you.' Speak slowly and pause after each point.

Step 6, Your turn: a survey of 50 students found 35 walk to school. Write the finding with its percentage. Answer: 'Of the 50 students surveyed, 35, or 70 percent, walk to school.' Check: 35 divided by 50 is 0.7, which is 70 percent.

modules.title: Unseen passages
modules.outcome: read faster and answer inference questions with evidence
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Unseen passages', taught in a way that is with notes, a worked line and a self-mark. The target is clear: read faster and answer inference questions with evidence. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.

modules.example: Solved: Passage: 'The old banyan tree gave shade to the whole village.' Q: what does 'shade' suggest? Protection from the sun. Inference: the tree matters to the villagers. Answer with a quote as evidence. Method: Model run for 'Unseen passages'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Read faster and answer inference questions with evidence: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Read this unseen passage. 'Mira checked the sky again. The washing was still on the line, but the wind had turned cold and the swallows were flying low. She looked at the dark edge of the hills, then at her mother.' First read it quickly for the general idea without stopping at hard words.

Step 2, Skim and scan. Skimming means reading fast for the main idea: Mira is worried about the weather. Scanning means hunting for one detail: ask 'What was on the line?' and your eye jumps to 'washing'. Read the question first, then scan the text for the matching word.

Step 3, Measure your speed. If you read a 240-word passage in 80 seconds, divide the words by seconds and multiply by 60: 240 divided by 80 is 3 words a second, so 180 words a minute. A comfortable target for this level is 200 or more, while still understanding it.

Step 4, Answer an inference question. 'What does Mira think will happen?' The passage never says rain. Gather clues: cold wind, low swallows, dark hills, washing still outside. Together they suggest a storm is coming. An inference is a sensible conclusion built from clues, not a guess.

Step 5, Write the answer with evidence. 'Mira thinks it will rain soon. The text says the wind "had turned cold" and the swallows were "flying low", which are signs of bad weather. She also checks the sky again, showing she is worried.' Notice the quoted words and the explanation.

Step 6, Your turn: why does Mira look at her mother? Model answer: She probably wants her mother to decide whether to bring in the washing. The text says she looked at the hills 'then at her mother', suggesting she is waiting for a reaction or a decision.

Method: Model run for 'Discussion and presentation'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. modules.standard: Prepare and deliver a presentation with slides: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Plan slides around one message. Topic: "Reducing plastic at school". Slide 1: title. Slide 2: the problem. Slide 3: two solutions. Slide 4: next steps. Reason: one slide, one idea.
Step 2, Write slide text in short phrases. Slide 3: "Reusable bottles; refill stations." Do not copy full paragraphs. Reason: the audience listens to you and reads only keywords.

Step 3, Use a script for spoken text. Say: "Every day, our canteen throws away about 200 plastic bottles. Over a month of school days, that is about 4,000 bottles." Reason: speaking adds information that the slide does not show.
Step 4, Choose a clear visual. A bar chart comparing bottles used: Monday 210, Tuesday 190, Wednesday 205. Label axes. Reason: a labelled chart is easier to interpret than a list of numbers.

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: reading the slide aloud word for word and facing the screen. Right: look at the audience, and say the key point in your own words. Another error: seven bullets on one slide. Right: two or three.
Step 6, Rehearse transitions. "Now that we have seen the problem, let's look at two solutions." "To conclude, small changes add up." Reason: transitions make the talk flow from slide to slide.

Step 7, Your turn. Plan a four-slide presentation on "Healthy lunch". Model answer: slide 1 title, slide 2 "Why lunch matters", slide 3 "Three healthy ideas: fruit, rice and beans, water", slide 4 "Make one change tomorrow".
